tagline: County seats and a rebuilt mansion along Alabama’s Governors’ Trail
intro: The Barbour County Governors’ Trail links Clio, Louisville and Clayton with Eufaula in approximately 36 miles. It is a journey through town centers, from Clio’s highway crossroads to downtown Clayton and the Shorter Mansion in Eufaula. Alabama Byways presents the route as a combination of governors’ history, historic sites and recreation, including nearby Blue Springs State Park and Lake Eufaula. Eufaula stands on the Chattahoochee River, and its historic district includes a concentration of buildings erected between 1870 and 1920, including commercial blocks, churches and houses.

A legislative act designated the trail in 2000 to recognize Barbour County residents who served as Alabama governors. The byway account identifies six governors and two others who served briefly as acting governors. That record includes John Gill Shorter’s role in writing the Confederate constitution and George C. Wallace’s stand at the University of Alabama to uphold segregation. The same account connects the county’s governors to education, railroad regulation and the promotion of farm-to-market roads.

Begin at the junction of SR 10 and SR 51 in Clio and travel northeast through Louisville to downtown Clayton. There the trail takes Highway 30 toward Eufaula, then turns north on US 431 to finish at Shorter Mansion.

moments.title: Louisville
moments.text: Louisville’s spelling changed, but its pronunciation remains Lewisville. Pike County made Louisville its seat in 1821; Barbour County chose it in 1832, giving this small town successive roles in two county governments. When Barbour County was formed from parts of Pike and Henry counties, Louisville became its first seat before that role passed to Clayton. Lumber became part of the town’s economy in 1828 and remains important; the Central of Georgia Railroad arrived in 1888. It lies six miles northeast of Clio and ten miles southwest of Clayton; the trail continues northeast to Clayton.

moments.title: Clayton
moments.text: Clayton’s center was laid out on a courthouse-square plan. Just south of the square, Grace Episcopal Church has white clapboard siding and a steeply pitched gable roof. Its building was completed in 1876, on land supplied by Henry DeLamar Clayton and his wife Victoria. The entry and its flanking windows have Gothic arched transoms. The town occupied the historic road from Hobdy’s Bridge over the Pea River to Eufaula on the Chattahoochee. The county seat also marks a turn in the drive: the Governors’ Trail leaves downtown Clayton on Highway 30 for Eufaula.
moments.notice: At Grace Episcopal Church, Gothic arched transoms top the entry and its flanking windows.

moments.title: Shorter Mansion
moments.text: Shorter Mansion’s present appearance came after a fire and several rounds of rebuilding. Eli Sims Shorter II and Wileyna Lamar Shorter built the original house in 1884–1885; it burned in 1895. T. H. Adams reconstructed it that year, and Jack McLeod’s 1906 renovations shaped the house seen today. Between the reconstruction and McLeod’s work, Eufaula architect C. A. Stevens modified the house in 1902–1903, adding another stage to its architectural history. In 1965 the Eufaula Heritage Association, formed to buy and restore the house, purchased it at auction. The association organized Eufaula’s first pilgrimage in 1966 and continues its historic-preservation work.
